candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: Philosophy's search for strict definitions and essential properties is ill suited to free will and should yield to population thinking.
candidates.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted answer follows the host's invitation and uses Dennett's characteristic critique of essentialism and definition-driven philosophy.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This methodological claim explains why the dispute persists and supports Dennett's broader effort to replace metaphysical essences with practically grounded capacities.
candidates.contextSummary: After the host asks why free will remains disputed after millennia, Dennett diagnoses a foundational methodological error in philosophy and recommends a Darwinian alternative.

candidates.speaker: Gregg Caruso
candidates.proposition: Free will remains disputed because it bears directly on responsibility and spans metaphysical, ethical, political, existential, and conceptual questions.
candidates.attributionBasis: The turn follows Dennett's opening answer and explicitly describes common ground between Caruso and Dennett before distinguishing several dimensions of the problem.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move establishes why definitions of free will, desert, and responsibility matter and frames the practical and conceptual terrain of Caruso's case.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Dennett's claim that philosophy's definition-centered method explains the debate's persistence.

candidates.contextSummary: Caruso supplements the methodological diagnosis by arguing that the issue persists because it crosses several philosophical domains and cannot be settled by science alone.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: Libertarian free will has no coherent model, and randomness cannot supply the relevant agency because the real issue is control rather than causation.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly condemns libertarianism, rejects soul-based agency, and develops a control-based treatment of classical and quantum randomness consistent with Dennett's position.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The argument removes libertarian alternatives while identifying control as the capacity that matters, thereby clearing the ground for Dennett's compatibilist account.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: The preceding discussion of libertarian theories and whether philosophical progress has improved them.

candidates.contextSummary: Following discussion of libertarian positions, Dennett argues that neither a nonphysical inner agent nor quantum chance produces freedom, while ordinary unpredictability can serve autonomous control.

candidates.speaker: Gregg Caruso
candidates.proposition: Introducing indeterminacy into deliberation does not create desert-grounding freedom because the agent still cannot settle which supported outcome occurs.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker distinguishes recent libertarian accounts and evaluates their strategically placed indeterminacy before concluding that agents lack the required control.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This supplies Caruso's control-based objection to naturalistic libertarianism and explains why reason-supported random outcomes cannot ground the responsibility at issue.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Dennett's dismissal of libertarian models and his claim that randomness does not provide control.

candidates.contextSummary: Caruso grants that sophisticated libertarian accounts improve on crude randomness but argues that replaying an indeterminate choice would expose an uncontrolled distribution of outcomes.

candidates.speaker: Gregg Caruso
candidates.proposition: Because persons and actions ultimately result from factors beyond their control, basic-desert responsibility is absent whether the universe is deterministic or indeterministic.
candidates.attributionBasis: Caruso explicitly identifies himself as the free-will skeptic, contrasts Dennett as the compatibilist, and states the defining thesis of his position.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is Caruso's core thesis connecting ultimate lack of control to denial of basic-desert responsibility independently of the truth of determinism.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: The host's pragmatic proposal that society might assume determinism even if individuals experience free choice.

candidates.contextSummary: In answering a pragmatic question, Caruso first defines his skepticism and separates it from a simple commitment to determinism, locating the dispute in basic desert.

candidates.speaker: Gregg Caruso
candidates.proposition: Practices that intentionally harm people on desert grounds require strong warrant for the requisite freedom, and unresolved disagreement leaves that burden unmet.
candidates.attributionBasis: Caruso introduces his epistemic argument, lays out its justificatory premise, applies it to punishment and blame, and states the resulting default against desert-based harm.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move converts skepticism about free will into a direct normative challenge to retribution while preserving the possibility of non-desert consequentialist measures.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: The host's suggestion that practical social benefits might justify adopting a useful assumption about free will.

candidates.contextSummary: Caruso argues that intentionally harmful responsibility practices are not innocuous and that proponents must justify the freedom and desert those practices presuppose.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: The freedom worth wanting is practical self-control, and responsibility-supporting laws and sanctions are necessary to sustain a secure cooperative society.
candidates.attributionBasis: The host hands the floor to Dennett, who invokes his own compatibilist framework and develops a sustained case from control, responsibility, social practices, and law.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This directly answers Caruso by grounding responsibility in observable capacities rather than metaphysical independence and by defending the social necessity of punishment.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Caruso's epistemic argument that uncertainty about desert makes intentionally harmful responsibility practices unjustified.

candidates.contextSummary: Dennett argues that responsibility tracks whether agents can control themselves, that capable agents must maintain that control, and that legal sanctions help secure social cooperation.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: Determinism does not eliminate the relevant ability to do otherwise because people can respond to persuasion, change their conduct, and develop moral competence.
candidates.attributionBasis: Dennett affirms the host's formulation and then explains a nonmetaphysical sense of alternatives through behavioral change, legal responsibility, and developing competence.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The argument directly supplies the reasons-responsive compatibilist capacity at the heart of the motion and rejects determinism as a barrier to genuine practical alternatives.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: The skeptical implication that determinism prevents agents from doing otherwise in a responsibility-grounding sense.

candidates.contextSummary: After the host asks whether controlled agents could have acted otherwise, Dennett identifies practical changeability and competence as the relevant basis for responsibility.

candidates.speaker: Gregg Caruso
candidates.proposition: Free-will skepticism denies only basic-desert responsibility for backward-looking praise, blame, punishment, and reward, not every form of responsibility.
candidates.attributionBasis: The host explicitly gives Caruso the floor, and Caruso carefully clarifies the limited responsibility concept denied by his own and allied skeptical positions.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The distinction blocks the claim that skepticism abolishes all responsibility and sharply defines the exact desert-based target of Caruso's challenge.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Dennett's contention that free-will skepticism encourages people to deny that anyone is ever responsible.

candidates.contextSummary: Caruso begins his response to Dennett by distinguishing basic-desert responsibility from other responsibility notions that skepticism can leave intact.
